body.text: In short:
Freedom of Information documents show Australia and China have signed an agreement to support each other's logistical operations in Antarctica this season.
China is planning an intercontinental ice runway in Antarctica that will cater for up to eight flights per season.
What's next?
China expects to open the runway in 2029–30.
Australia has signed a logistics cooperation agreement with China as the country continues to expand its presence in Antarctica, including plans for an intercontinental runway.
The new agreement was revealed in a Senate estimates brief prepared for the environment department last month and released to the ABC under Freedom of Information (FOI) laws.

"Australia and China have a history of logistical and scientific cooperation, particularly through AAD [Australian Antarctic Division] and the Polar Research Institute of China [PRIC]," the brief states.

"While the AAD and PRIC did not enter into a cooperative agreement for the 2025–26 Antarctic season, an agreement covering mutually beneficial logistics cooperation during the 2026–27 season is in development."
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) told the ABC the agreement has since been enacted.
"International collaboration underpins the Antarctic Treaty system and its objective of maintaining Antarctica as a place of peace, science and environmental protection," a DFAT spokesperson said.
"Australia and China have a long-standing collaborative relationship on Antarctic matters, including logistical cooperation, the specific nature of which varies season to season."
Specific details about the new agreement were not provided, however, the ABC understands it is a type of "quid pro quo" (QPQ) arrangement.
QPQ arrangements allow the parties to support each other's operational activities, including aviation and ground transportation, as well as emergency assistance.
Australia's last QPQ agreement with China was in 2024–25.
Australia has similar Antarctic-related QPQ arrangements with other countries, including France.
Runway will be 'aircraft carrier-style hub', China says
The Senate estimates brief also includes references to China's expanding presence in Antarctica, which now totals five research stations and plans for a sixth.
Additionally, the brief notes China's plans to build a new intercontinental ice runway within Australian Antarctic Territory (AAT).
"An environmental evaluation for a blue ice intercontinental runway in the Grove Mountains [inside the AAT] was made available by China in December 2025," the brief note says.

"For environmental assessments at this level, proponent Parties are not required to seek international views, but we note that China has made this evaluation public on the Antarctic Treaty Secretariat [ATS] website," the brief states.
The environmental evaluation says the runway will cater for up to eight flights per year, carrying 30 passengers and 15 tonnes of cargo.
It says it is expected to open in 2029/30, and would enhance exploration and research capabilities and create a new backup aviation facility for other countries that fly in the region.

"The proposed blue-ice runway at the Grove Mountains, leveraging its superior geographical location and capability to support wheeled aircraft operations, will serve as an advanced inland 'forward base' and an 'aircraft carrier-style hub' for East Antarctica," the evaluation states.
Under the Antarctic Treaty, countries are allowed to establish research facilities and stations anywhere in Antarctica.
China carried out preliminary work at the runway site during the 2025/26 summer, including snow removal, surface levelling and environmental monitoring.
China currently relies primarily on ships to transport its expeditioners and equipment to Antarctica.
In 2023, it built a ski way at Zhongshan Station, but it can only handle smaller aircraft.
China's new runway would be similar to Australia's ice runway at Wilkins Aerodrome, which caters for intercontinental jets.
The ABC asked DFAT whether Australia supported China's new runway, or had any concerns about it, but a spokesperson only provided a general response.

"Australia expects all parties to comply with the requirements of the Antarctic Treaty and its Environmental Protocol, including non-militarisation, freedom of scientific investigation, international cooperation, environmental protection, and the mining ban."
Tasmania seeks more Chinese icebreaker visits
One of China's icebreakers, Xue Long, docked in Hobart last week to refuel and collect supplies ahead of its voyage to Antarctica.
The ship's visit came after the Premier Jeremy Rockliff led a Tasmanian delegation to China earlier this month.
One of the objectives of the trade mission was to encourage China to increase the number of port visits its icebreakers make in Hobart.
For the past two years, the Xue Long and Xue Long 2 have been making about two visits each year, but there is the potential for three or four visits per year.

"Discussions centred on Tasmania's established relationship with China's Antarctic program, and Hobart's role as a gateway to Antarctica, including opportunities associated with Antarctic science, logistics and support services," a Building Tasmania spokesperson said.
No outcomes in relation to Antarctica have been announced following the trade mission.
Defence rejects FOI application on national security grounds

Over the past two years, the Chinese icebreakers have attracted the attention of US authorities during their passage to the Arctic, with the US Coast Guard tracking them "to rapidly respond to any detected malign activity".
Earlier this year, the ABC submitted FOI requests for documents relating to the ships' port access in Hobart and Fremantle, where they had previously been docking until 2024.
However, the FOI applications were rejected by both the Defence Department and DFAT on national security grounds.

"The documents contain information concerning the Commonwealth's consideration of foreign vessel access to Australian ports in circumstances involving matters of national security sensitivity," Defence said in its statement of reasons.

"Disclosure could reasonably be expected to cause damage to the security of the Commonwealth by exposing information that would enable inferences to be drawn about Australia's security priorities, threat perceptions and strategic interests in relation to foreign maritime activity."
The ABC contacted the Chinese Embassy for comment but did not receive a response.
